entities.name: Basilica of St. Martin, Tours
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Basilica of Saint Martin of Tours in Tours, France — built over the tomb of Saint Martin of Tours (c. 316-397 CE), the Roman soldier turned monk who became Bishop of Tours and is the patron saint of France — is one of the most important pilgrimage sites in medieval Christianity. The original basilica, built by Bishop Perpetuus c. 470-490 CE, became the wealthiest and most visited pilgrimage church in medieval France; the current Neo-Byzantine basilica (1886-1924) replaces the medieval structure largely destroyed during the French Revolution.

Saint Martin of Tours is one of the most consequential figures in Western Christianity: the story of his dividing his military cloak to share with a naked beggar (giving rise to the word 'chapel' from his 'capella' — small cloak — kept as a sacred relic carried into battle by Frankish kings) is one of Christianity's most famous acts of charity. Martin was the first non-martyr to be venerated as a saint in the Western church, and his cult — spread by his biographer Sulpicius Severus's Vita Martini (c. 397 CE) — was the most popular saint cult in early medieval Europe.

The Via Turonensis (one of the four French Camino de Santiago routes) begins at Saint Martin's basilica in Tours — pilgrimages to Santiago often began with a pilgrimage to Tours — making the basilica one of the starting points of the entire Camino de Santiago tradition. Alcuin of York, the great scholar of the Carolingian Renaissance, served as abbot of Saint Martin's from 796-804 CE and wrote many of his works there. The medieval basilica was one of the greatest in Europe before its Revolutionary destruction.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Basilica of Saint Martin of Tours — tomb of France's patron saint, etymological origin of the word 'chapel', starting point of the Via Turonensis (French Camino), and Alcuin's Carolingian intellectual center — is one of medieval France's most historically consequential sacred sites.
